about.title: About this site
about.unofficial: UoA World Model is made by a student for students. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by or maintained by the University of Auckland, and it uses no University logos or branding. For anything that matters, check the University's own campus maps and your own timetable in Student Services Online.
about.what: It answers two questions: which building and floor is my room in, and is a class timetabled in this room right now. Type a room code, a building or a course into Search, or click a building to step inside and browse floors and rooms.
about.whatNoTimetable: It answers one question today: which building and floor is my room in. Type a room code from your timetable or a building name into Search, or click a building to step inside and browse floors and rooms. It is also built to show what is timetabled in a room at any moment, but class times are not available yet; see Known limitations below.
about.whatBuildings: It shows the buildings in 3D on the real ground, with their names, codes and heights. Type a building's name or code into Search, or click a building to see what is known about it. Floors, rooms and class times are not shown; see Known limitations below.
about.whatBuildingsNames: It shows the buildings in 3D on the real ground, with their names and heights. Type a building's name into Search, or click a building to see what is known about it. Floors, rooms and class times are not shown; see Known limitations below.
about.how: Drag to rotate. Scroll or pinch to zoom. Right-drag, Shift-drag or use two fingers to move. Click a building to open it, then pick a floor and a room. The address bar always holds a link to exactly what you are looking at.
about.howBuildings: Drag to rotate. Scroll or pinch to zoom. Right-drag, Shift-drag or use two fingers to move. Click a building to see its name, code and height. The address bar always holds a link to exactly what you are looking at.
about.howBuildingsNames: Drag to rotate. Scroll or pinch to zoom. Right-drag, Shift-drag or use two fingers to move. Click a building to see its name and height. The address bar always holds a link to exactly what you are looking at.

limits.timetable: No class times yet. The University's timetable can no longer be read without signing in: the guest class search has been retired and the official Classes API needs credentials. Until the site's maintainer supplies those, this site shows rooms and buildings but cannot say what is scheduled in them. Nothing here is made up to fill the gap.
limits.timetableLoaded: Class times come from a snapshot of the timetable taken on {date}. Rooms and times change during the semester; your own timetable is the authority.
limits.scheduled: A timetabled class is not the same as an occupied room. Classes are cancelled, moved and recorded online, and rooms are used for things that are not on the timetable.
limits.heights: Each building is stacked floor by floor from the outlines on the official campus map, so its podiums, towers, setbacks and courtyards are real. Floors whose outlines differ by less than a twentieth of their area are drawn as one block. Its height is not surveyed: every floor is drawn {height} m high. The windows and the rim round each roof are drawn by rule and say nothing about the real walls and roofs. The ground's heights come from Land Information New Zealand's 8 m elevation model of 2012, which is drawn from contours: it is smooth bare ground, with sharp peaks a few metres low and the reclaimed waterfront a few metres high. A building's ground floor stands at the ground under its middle, never more than 4 m above its lowest corner; on a slope its uphill side goes into the hill and a footing fills the gap below the other side. Floors under the ground floor are not drawn from outside; opened, they lie under the ground, {height} m apart like the rest, and the ground is drawn see-through over them. The buildings drawn in detail and the measured massings (above) are the exception: from outside, their shape and height are measured, except where a building under works keeps its estimated block (above).
limits.rooms: Outlines are simplified from the official campus map. Learning spaces (lecture theatres, teaching rooms, labs, studios, study spaces) are named and can be selected. Every other space on the campus map is drawn as a shape with no code or name, so that a floor reads as a floor plan, and its floor is tinted by the campus map's type for it: offices, other labs, toilets, stairs and lifts, services, and areas the map does not describe. Point at a shape, or tap it, to read that type in the campus map's own words. Stairs, lifts, toilets and showers carry a sign. A room among them is found by its code and marked with a pin, and the shape it stands on is outlined. Walls stand on every outline at a height chosen for the drawing; the campus map has no wall heights and no doors, so none are shown. Floors where people live and childcare centres are left blank, and single parking bays are not drawn. Some floors are blank or nearly blank on the campus map itself, most of them in halls of residence; the floor list marks them and the building bar says so. The furniture drawn in a selected room is decoration laid out by rule; it is not a seating plan and says nothing about capacity.
limits.campuses: Every campus on the official campus map is modelled in 3D. The City, Grafton and Newmarket campuses share one stretch of the city; Tai Tokerau, Tai Tonga, Leigh, Waiheke and Ardmore, and one Grafton building on Carrick Place, each stand in their own patch of surroundings, a few hundred metres across, and the map jumps between them. Positions far from the City Campus are drawn on the same flat map, so shapes at Tai Tokerau, 125 km north, are about 1.4% narrower east to west than they are. The sea is not drawn: OpenStreetMap maps the coast as a line, which this map does not turn into water, so Leigh and Waiheke stand on land to the edge of their patch.
limits.context: Surrounding buildings, streets and trees come from OpenStreetMap. Where it maps a building in parts or gives a roof a shape, those are drawn, the roof in a simplified form. Where a height is not mapped, a default is used. In the walker views every building but those drawn in detail, the University's and the rest, is drawn with storeys from its height, windows, and walls of plaster, brick, concrete, stone, glass or weatherboard chosen by rule from where it stands; none of it says what a real building looks like, and there are no doors, since none are mapped. The ground there is drawn by rule as well, on the streets, paths, railways, parks and ponds OpenStreetMap maps: asphalt with white lines, kerbs, paving slabs, steps, sleepers and rails, lawns and water, and grass and bare earth elsewhere. Its widths, lines and kerbs say nothing about the real ones, and there are no crossings, arrows or signs, since none are mapped. A tree standing alone is where OpenStreetMap maps it; its size and shape are drawn by rule, and in the walker views so are its leaves, its bark and the way it sways in a light breeze, the same every day; none of it says what kind of tree it is. Trees OpenStreetMap tags as deciduous turn in April and May, stand bare from June to August and come into leaf in September and October; the rest are drawn evergreen. Trees inside woodland areas are scattered for decoration.
limits.walker: The walker is a made-up figure, not a person: it stands for nobody, and nothing about where it goes leaves your browser. Its walks are planned round the buildings on the map and along OpenStreetMap's paths and streets, off motorways except over footbridges. Doors and entrances are not mapped, so a walk to a building ends beside its nearest wall, and it passes gates, fences and kerbs the map does not have. Its body is the "Animated Human" model by Quaternius, given to the public domain (CC0); its stance, trainers, hair, mouth, backpack and umbrella are drawn here by rule, in colours that are none of the University's. Where a building or a tree hides it, its shape shows through. It can also ride a made-up electric scooter on the same ways, at up to 25 km/h, or fly a made-up drone in its place, up to 120 m above the ground and over the roofs as high as the map draws them, which for most buildings are estimated. Neither is any real make, and their colours are the project's own. An agent can steer it on your own computer through the scripts in the source code. The walk has a game, Study Quest, off until you start it: its villains (the DDL, Procrastination, Distraction, Plagiarism, Exam Anxiety and the Final Exam), its books, notes and coffee and its quests are made up. None of them is anything on the campus or stands for a real class, course, person, room or due date; a quest names a building only as a place to go. Its progress is kept only until you close the page; its best grade and its settings stay in your browser, and nothing leaves it.
limits.calendar: Semester dates are transcribed by hand from the 2026 University Calendar. Dates for 2027 were not fully published when this was built.
limits.subjects: The list of subject codes comes from the 2026 University Calendar.
limits.daylight: The sun stands where it does over the City Campus at the date and time shown, from NOAA's published solar-position equations; below 10° above the horizon it is drawn at 10°, so that shadows stay on the map. Night falls as the sun goes from 6° above the horizon to 8° below. In Now mode the cloud, rain and fog follow Open-Meteo's current weather for the City Campus, and the falling rain is drawn by rule; Preview shows a clear sky, because past and future weather are not known here.

about.privacy: The site has no accounts and sets no cookies. Staff names are deliberately left out. Only the copy at campusworldmodel.com is counted: there Cloudflare, which serves the site, counts page views and visits with its Web Analytics. It stores nothing in your browser and does not record which building or room you look at; a content blocker may stop it. If the weather line is shown, your browser asks Open-Meteo for the current weather in Auckland; nothing about you is sent beyond that request. A walk with the walker stays in your browser: where it goes, what it says and what it wears are not sent anywhere. The walk's game keeps its best grade and its sound and motion settings in your browser's own storage, and sends nothing anywhere.
about.osm: Map context © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License.
about.landmarks: Drawn in detail from code: {buildings}. Their sizes come from the Auckland Part 1 LiDAR point cloud of 2024, captured by Woolpert for Regional Software Holdings Limited and distributed by OpenTopography and Land Information New Zealand. It is licensed by Regional Software Holdings Limited for re-use under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence. AI agents drew their details and compared them with Google Street View photographs, and the Kate Edger Information Commons, the Humanities Building, buildings 302, 303 and 303S of the Science Centre, Architecture - West, Architecture - East, Building 907, Auckland Bioengineering House, the Sir Owen G Glenn Building, 49 Symonds Street, Okareta, buildings 501, 502, 505 and 507 of the M&HS Building, Te Pūtahi Tangata, the George Mason Biology Building, 2-6 Park Ave, Building 114, 67 Symonds Street, Fine Arts Studio Block 431, Fine Arts Studio Block 433, 58 Symonds Street, Security, Building 903 and Structures Hall each with another photograph of it, none of which are published here; where trees hide a building from the photographs, its shape was checked against the LiDAR from above, and what no photograph shows is drawn plainly or after the parts that are shown. A size that nothing measures, such as the underside of the Clock Tower East Wing's link, is estimated, and its building's card says so. Where every source shows a building during building works, only the part that the photographs show as it stands is drawn in detail, and the rest keeps the map's estimated block. On the map they take the map's colours when you come near them. From a walker's height they are drawn in their own materials, such as stone, brick, concrete, painted render and timber, glass, slate, clay tiles and metal, on a computer with a graphics card, and in the map's colours on phones and on computers without one. A click on them still opens their floors.
about.measured: Measured by LiDAR and drawn by rule: {buildings}. Their heights and roofs come from the same LiDAR, measured by a program, and they stand in place of their blocks when you come near them. Their walls, storeys and windows are drawn by rule, not from photographs. A click on them still opens their floors. The heights of all other buildings, and of the part of a building under works that keeps its block, are estimated from their floors.
about.landmarksOtherSource: Some of the sizes of {buildings} come from {credit}; the building's card says which.
about.inspiration: This site was inspired by the Tsinghua World Model, an independent student project that lets you walk through Tsinghua University's campus and find courses and classrooms in it. The idea of a campus you can step into comes from there. The code, models and data here were made separately.
about.code: The code is open source under the MIT licence. If a room is in the wrong place, please open an issue.

walker.note: A made-up figure, scooter and drone: none stands for a real one, and where they go stays in your browser. The scooter keeps to the same ways as a walk; the drone flies up to {ceiling} m above the ground and over the roofs, as high as the map draws them, which for most buildings are estimated. Doors are not mapped, so a walk ends beside the nearest side of a building, and inside it keeps to corridors where it can.
